nodes.label: Replication: clusters, replicas and how many copies

card.definition: Replication keeps multiple copies of the same data on several servers of a cluster, so the system keeps serving when one server fails. How many replicas to keep trades performance against the risk of losing data.

keyFacts.text: A cluster is a set of coordinated servers working together.
keyFacts.quote: A set of coordinated servers working together.

keyFacts.text: Replication means keeping multiple copies of data for availability.
keyFacts.quote: Keeping multiple copies of data for availability.

keyFacts.text: Replication saves multiple copies of data across the cluster, which gives high availability.
keyFacts.quote: Replication saves multiple copies of data across the cluster, which gives high availability.

keyFacts.text: Fewer replicas: better performance but a higher risk of losing data; use them when data is easy to regenerate and reload.
keyFacts.quote: Use when data is easy to regenerate and reload.

keyFacts.text: More replicas: less likely to lose data but possibly lower performance; use them when you have little tolerance for data loss.
keyFacts.quote: Use when you have little tolerance for data loss.

keyFacts.text: Many replicas bring higher availability, durability and read throughput, at the cost of more storage, slower writes and harder consistency.
keyFacts.quote: Cons are more storage, slower writes and harder consistency.

keyFacts.text: A lone server with an idle backup wastes capacity: the backup does no useful work until a failure.
keyFacts.quote: reserved capacity that does no useful work until a failure

keyFacts.text: In a multi-server cluster with replicated data, the remaining servers carry the full workload when one fails; performance may dip but the app stays up.
keyFacts.quote: the others carry the full workload, performance may dip, but the app stays up

keyFacts.text: Scaling out (adding servers) is more flexible than scaling up (a bigger single server).
keyFacts.quote: Scaling out is more flexible than scaling up

nodes.label: Master-slave replication: one writer, many readers

card.definition: In master-slave replication one master node accepts the writes and replica (slave) nodes serve the reads. It scales read-heavy workloads well, but the single write point is both a bottleneck and a risk. Redis works this way.

keyFacts.text: One master node accepts writes.
keyFacts.quote: One master node accepts writes

keyFacts.text: Many slave (replica) nodes serve reads.
keyFacts.quote: Many slave/replica nodes serve reads

keyFacts.text: Master-slave replication scales read-heavy workloads well.
keyFacts.quote: Scales read-heavy workloads well

keyFacts.text: The single write point is a bottleneck and a risk.
keyFacts.quote: Single write point = bottleneck & risk

keyFacts.text: Read-heavy example: fans refreshing a live score site make many reads and few writes.
keyFacts.quote: fans refreshing a live score site many reads, few writes

keyFacts.text: When the master fails, the remaining nodes elect a new master; when a slave fails, the other slaves keep serving reads.
keyFacts.quote: Remaining nodes elect a new master

keyFacts.text: Redis is the course's example of master-slave replication.
keyFacts.quote: Redis uses master-slave replication.

keyFacts.text: In Redis a replica is configured with replicaof and inspected with INFO replication.
keyFacts.quote: configure master-slave replication with replicaof and inspect it with INFO replication

keyFacts.text: In the lab (native install) the master listens on 127.0.0.1 port 6379 and the replicas use 6380 and 6381.
keyFacts.quote: the master is 127.0.0.1 6379, replicas use 6380 and 6381

keyFacts.text: Manual failover: REPLICAOF NO ONE promotes a replica to master.
keyFacts.quote: REPLICAOF NO ONE

keyFacts.text: The derby sizing task expects 250,000 score reads per second and 5 writes per second.
keyFacts.quote: 250,000 score reads per second and 5 writes per second

card.definition: In masterless replication every node accepts reads and writes, so writes scale too and there is no single master to lose. The price: the database must handle write conflicts between nodes. Partitions are often organised in a ring where each write also lands on the owning node's two neighbours.

keyFacts.text: In masterless replication all nodes accept reads and writes.
keyFacts.quote: All nodes accept reads and writes

keyFacts.text: Masterless replication scales writes, not just reads, and gives higher availability.
keyFacts.quote: Scales writes, not just reads

keyFacts.text: A masterless database must handle write conflicts between nodes.
keyFacts.quote: Must handle write conflicts between nodes

keyFacts.text: In a masterless cluster there is no single master to lose; other nodes take over a failed node's reads and writes.
keyFacts.quote: Other nodes take over its reads and writes

keyFacts.text: Riak is the course's example of a masterless database.
keyFacts.quote: Example | Redis | Riak

keyFacts.text: A ring is a logical structure for organising partitions: each node is linked to its two neighbours.
keyFacts.quote: each node is linked to its two neighbours

keyFacts.text: Ring example: a hash-like function maps each key to 0-95 and 8 servers each own a range of 12 values.
keyFacts.quote: 8 servers each own a range of 12 values

keyFacts.text: Each write goes to the owning node and its two neighbours, giving high availability.
keyFacts.quote: Each write goes to the owning node and its two neighbours, giving high availability.

keyFacts.text: When S4 fails, S3 and S5 answer reads and accept writes for S4's data, then send S4 the writes it missed when it comes back.
keyFacts.quote: S4 comes back: S3 and S5 send it the writes it missed.

keyFacts.text: The typical key-value cluster is masterless (peer-to-peer), often arranged as a ring, with no single point of failure.
keyFacts.quote: Every node is equal, so there is no single point of failure.

anchors.quote: A ring is a logical structure for organizing partitions

nodes.label: The CAP theorem, two meanings of consistency and the two-phase commit

card.definition: The CAP theorem (Brewer's theorem) says a distributed database cannot guarantee consistency, availability and partition protection all at the same time. Keeping a primary and a backup consistent with a two-phase commit works, but every write waits for both servers.

keyFacts.text: A distributed database cannot guarantee consistency, availability and partition protection all at the same time.
keyFacts.quote: A distributed database cannot guarantee all three of these at the same time

keyFacts.text: The CAP theorem is also called Brewer's theorem.
keyFacts.quote: The CAP Theorem (Brewer's Theorem)

keyFacts.text: Consistency: all servers hold the same, current data.
keyFacts.quote: All servers hold the same, current data.

keyFacts.text: Availability: every query gets a response.
keyFacts.quote: Every query gets a response.

keyFacts.text: Partition protection: the system works even if the network splits servers apart.
keyFacts.quote: Works even if the network splits servers apart.

keyFacts.text: Transaction consistency: a change leaves the data in a valid state.
keyFacts.quote: Transaction consistency, a change leaves the data in a valid state.

keyFacts.text: Replica consistency: copies of data on different servers hold the same values.
keyFacts.quote: Replica consistency, copies of data on different servers hold the same values.

keyFacts.text: Two-phase commit: commit to the primary server, then to the backup server; the transaction commits only when both succeed.
keyFacts.quote: keep a primary and a backup, and write to both

keyFacts.text: If either write fails, the whole transaction rolls back, so the two servers stay consistent.
keyFacts.quote: If either write fails, the whole transaction rolls back

keyFacts.text: The price of the two-phase commit: a write is not finished until both servers confirm.
keyFacts.quote: a write is not finished until both servers confirm

keyFacts.text: CA assumes no partition (two-phase commit); CP blocks some queries; AP may return stale data (the cart).
keyFacts.quote: Available + partition-tolerant, may return stale data (the cart).

keyFacts.text: Partitions are rare on local networks, so designers mostly trade consistency against availability.
keyFacts.quote: designers mostly trade consistency against availability

card.definition: A quorum is the number of servers that must respond for a read or a write to count as complete. The read threshold trades response time against consistency; the write threshold trades response time against durability.

keyFacts.text: A quorum is the number of servers that must respond for a read or write to count as complete.
keyFacts.quote: the number of servers that must respond for a read or write to count as complete

keyFacts.text: With a quorum, servers effectively vote on the answer.
keyFacts.quote: Servers effectively "vote" on the answer.

keyFacts.text: The read threshold trades response time against consistency.
keyFacts.quote: Read threshold → response vs. consistency

keyFacts.text: With 5 replicas, a read threshold of 1 is fastest but may return stale data.
keyFacts.quote: threshold 1 is fastest but may return stale data

keyFacts.text: With 5 replicas, a read threshold of 5 guarantees a consistent read but is slowest.
keyFacts.quote: threshold 5 guarantees a consistent read but is slowest

keyFacts.text: A middle read threshold, for example 3 of 5, lets the servers agree by majority.
keyFacts.quote: A middle value (e.g., 3) lets servers agree by majority

keyFacts.text: The write threshold trades response time against durability.
keyFacts.quote: Write threshold → response vs. durability

keyFacts.text: A write threshold of 1 is fast but risky: lose that server and the data is gone.
keyFacts.quote: Threshold 1 is fast but risky, lose that server and the data is gone.

keyFacts.text: A write threshold of at least 2, with more replicas than the threshold, protects durability without slowing writes much.
keyFacts.quote: protects durability without slowing writes much

keyFacts.text: Example: write to 3 replicas and wait for 2 acks; the third is written in the background.
keyFacts.quote: Success returned after 2 acks; the app moves on.

keyFacts.text: Example read: wait for 2 matching answers; replica 3 answers v1 (stale), two agree on v2, so v2 is returned.
keyFacts.quote: Two agree: return v2 to the application.

keyFacts.text: A higher read quorum gives fresher data, at the cost of higher latency.
keyFacts.quote: A higher read quorum gives fresher data, at the cost of higher latency.

nodes.label: ACID versus BASE and the strengths of eventual consistency

card.definition: ACID is the relational model's strict transaction guarantee; BASE (Basically Available, Soft State, Eventually Consistent) is the looser NoSQL model in which copies may differ briefly and then converge. Eventual consistency comes in several strengths: causal, read-your-writes, session, monotonic read and monotonic write.

keyFacts.text: ACID belongs to the relational model: strong, strict guarantees on every transaction, correctness first.
keyFacts.quote: Strong, strict guarantees on every transaction, correctness first.

keyFacts.text: BASE is common to NoSQL: looser guarantees that favour availability and speed at scale.
keyFacts.quote: Looser guarantees that favor availability and speed at scale.

keyFacts.text: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.
keyFacts.quote: Atomicity · Consistency · Isolation · Durability

keyFacts.text: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft State, Eventually Consistent.
keyFacts.quote: Basically Available · Soft State · Eventually Consistent

keyFacts.text: Basically available: a partial failure is tolerated and the rest of the system keeps serving.
keyFacts.quote: A partial failure is tolerated, the rest of the system keeps serving.

keyFacts.text: Soft state: a value may be overwritten by more recent data later on.
keyFacts.quote: a value may be overwritten by more recent data later on

keyFacts.text: Eventually consistent: copies may differ briefly, then converge once replication catches up.
keyFacts.quote: Copies may differ briefly, then converge to the same value once replication catches up.

keyFacts.text: Causal consistency: all copies reflect the order in which updates happened.
keyFacts.quote: All copies reflect the order in which updates happened

keyFacts.text: Read-your-writes: once you write a value, your own reads always return it.
keyFacts.quote: Once you write a value, your own reads always return it

keyFacts.text: Session consistency: read-your-writes holds, but only within one session.
keyFacts.quote: Read-your-writes holds, but only within one session.

keyFacts.text: Monotonic read: once you have seen a value, you never see an earlier version of it.
keyFacts.quote: Once you have seen a value, you will never see an earlier version of it

keyFacts.text: Monotonic write: your writes execute in the order you issued them, essential when operations don't commute.
keyFacts.quote: Your writes execute in the order you issued them, essential when operations don't commute.

keyFacts.text: Charlie's bill: discount then order gives $2,000; order then discount gives $1,890.

anchors.quote: Two Transaction Models: ACID vs. BASE

nodes.label: Synthesis: choose replication and consistency for a scenario

card.definition: Put every step together on real cases: a bank needs consistency and availability at all times, a shopping cart accepts a short window of inconsistency for speed, a ride-hailing app must split its choice during a network fault, and a live-score site is read-heavy.

keyFacts.text: Bank and financial systems need both consistency and availability at all times: a two-phase commit is worth the extra time.
keyFacts.quote: A two-phase commit is worth the extra time, a wrong balance is unacceptable.

keyFacts.text: An e-commerce cart writes to one server, confirms to the shopper and replicates to the others in the background.
keyFacts.quote: Write to one server, confirm to the shopper, and replicate to the others in the background

keyFacts.text: Eventual consistency means accepting a short window of inconsistency in return for speed, trusting the copies to converge.
keyFacts.quote: accept a short window of inconsistency in return for speed, trusting the copies to converge

keyFacts.text: Ride-hailing exercise: a network fault cuts the link between the two replicas for 90 seconds.
keyFacts.quote: A network fault cuts the link between them for 90 seconds.

keyFacts.text: In the ride-hailing exercise the surge-price display tolerates small staleness, but the payment step must never double-charge a rider.
keyFacts.quote: the surge-price display tolerates small staleness, but the payment / charge step must never double-charge a rider

keyFacts.text: The live-score scenario has many reads and very few writes.
keyFacts.quote: many reads, very few writes

keyFacts.text: In the masterless conflict scenario, two journalists send different values for the same key to two nodes at 21:47:03.
keyFacts.quote: At 21:47:03, journalist A sends match:1001:homeGoals = 2 to node 1
